claims.claim: Robin Sloan writes that the AI companies may wreck every creative industry and flood the internet with garbage while culture fades into a sort of oatmeal sludge.
claims.source: Robin Sloan, novelist, robinsloan.com lab blog, 2025
claims.page: section following 'What if that isn't the primary application?'

claims.feature: other: writing produced for a real reason
claims.claim: Sloan hypothesises that commissioned training text would lack the grain and umami of writing actually produced for its own varied reasons.
claims.source: Robin Sloan, novelist, robinsloan.com lab blog, 2025
claims.quote: The same grain. The same umami.
claims.page: section on commissioning a clean-room corpus

claims.claim: Neil Clarke asserts that generative AI use differs from plagiarism in that proving it to a legal standard is significantly more complex, since few leave a prompt in or admit what they did.
claims.quote: proving it to a legal standard is significantly more complex
claims.page: body, on why editors should not name names

claims.claim: Clarke states that a handful of publishers are willing to publish generated slop and that at minimum they should be transparent about it.
claims.quote: There are a handful of publishers that are ok with generated slop.
claims.page: final bullet, 'YOU MAY DISCOVER THEY DO NOT CARE'

claims.feature: other: the first draft is not the same object
claims.claim: Ted Chiang argues that a writer's first draft is not an unoriginal idea expressed clearly but an original idea expressed poorly.
claims.quote: it’s an original idea expressed poorly
claims.page: section on using models as a starting point for original writing

claims.feature: other: revision is where quality is made
claims.claim: Chiang holds that the dissatisfaction accompanying a human first draft is what directs rewriting, and that this is one of the things lacking when a writer starts from generated text.
claims.quote: your awareness of the distance between what it says and what you want

claims.feature: other: surface polish with nothing underneath
claims.claim: Chiang argues that because a model rephrases rather than quotes, it creates the illusion that it understands the material.
claims.quote: it creates the illusion that ChatGPT understands the material
claims.page: section on lossy versus lossless compression

claims.feature: other: surface polish with nothing underneath
claims.claim: Chiang states that when dealing with sequences of words, lossy compression looks smarter than lossless compression.
claims.quote: lossy compression looks smarter than lossless compression
claims.page: section on lossy versus lossless compression

claims.claim: Chiang concludes from GPT-3's arithmetic failures that its statistical analysis produces a superficial approximation of the real thing and no more.
claims.quote: a superficial approximation of the real thing

claims.claim: Chiang predicted that the more model-generated text is published, the more the Web becomes a blurrier version of itself.
claims.quote: the more the Web becomes a blurrier version of itself
claims.page: section on generating Web content and content mills

claims.claim: Mark Williams ran the opening paragraphs of The Cuckoo's Calling through six free AI-detection tools and got three entirely different verdicts, from ZeroGPT's 50.9% AI-generated and TextGuard's 73% to three tools returning 100% human.
claims.source: Mark Williams, editor of The New Publishing Standard, 2026
claims.quote: Six tools. The same text. Three entirely different verdicts.

claims.claim: Williams reports that Quillbot rated the 1965 Gambian national anthem 100% AI-generated while rating actual AI output 100% human.
claims.source: Mark Williams, editor of The New Publishing Standard, 2026
claims.quote: formal ceremonial writing is, by design, controlled and consistent
claims.page: sections 'The Experiment' and 'How The Tools Actually Work'

claims.claim: Williams states that AI models optimised for coherence tend toward uniform sentence lengths, typically fifteen to twenty-five words, with consistent grammatical structures.
claims.source: Mark Williams, editor of The New Publishing Standard, 2026
claims.page: section 'How The Tools Actually Work', on burstiness

claims.claim: Williams argues that highly polished, professionally edited, obsessively revised human prose looks like AI prose to perplexity-and-burstiness detectors, so the very qualities writing teachers praise produce the flagged signature.
claims.source: Mark Williams, editor of The New Publishing Standard, 2026
claims.quote: Highly polished, professionally edited, obsessively revised human prose looks like AI prose

claims.claim: Williams reports that The Gettysburg Address scores as high-probability AI-generated on multiple mainstream detection tools.
claims.source: Mark Williams, editor of The New Publishing Standard, 2026
claims.quote: The Gettysburg Address scores as high-probability AI-generated on multiple mainstream detection tools.
